findings.text: The first paragraph covers what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves, in plain words. A newcomer could repeat it after one read.
findings.source: Header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The second section a newcomer reaches is an error message. The page promises a commit traced to models, cost and verdict, and this is the one spot that should show it, so the error weakens the page's main claim. The raw internal error text adds nothing for this reader.
findings.source: Check it on a real job: "The records of job 20261029-073603-7kqv could not be read here, so no models, verdict or costs are shown: no reading record for job 20261029-073603-7kqv."

findings.text: The page is titled after firstmate, but firstmate is not explained until the "Start here" section. A visitor who came for Athena may at first think they are on the wrong project's site.
findings.source: Page title and h1: "Athena explains how firstmate handles work"; lede: "Athena made this study of firstmate..."

findings.text: This link is for the site owner, yet it sits in the header beside the newcomer's next step. A first-time reader cannot use it, and "your decision" is misleading for them.
findings.source: Header: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The next steps are concrete and runnable: prerequisites, clone, install and a first command, and the header links to them. The prerequisites line comes after the clone step, though a reader needs it first.
findings.source: Next steps: "Get the code: git clone ...", "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm", "Install Athena from the checkout: ./setup.sh", "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: Most of the page is a detailed state-machine study of firstmate. It shows the claim-to-source tracing well, but a newcomer has to read a lot about another tool to see the point, and labels like "t9" and "ra1" mean nothing to them.
findings.source: Transitions section (cards t1 to t12) and "Why it is built this way" (cards ra1 to ra6)

findings.text: Every statement links to a claim, and every claim links to exact file lines at a pinned commit. This shows the traceability the lede promises, and a curious newcomer can check it.
findings.source: Claims and sources, e.g. claim c3 linking "bin/fm-spawn.sh:194-197" at the pinned commit

findings.text: The page is honest about gaps, but several glossary entries say only that a term is undefined. A newcomer looking these words up learns little.
findings.source: Glossary: "The firstmate source does not define a heartbeat." / "does not define an endpoint" / "does not define a wake"
